findings.source: NVIDIA IsaacGymEnvs (legacy Isaac Gym preview envs, repo now under isaac-sim org) — AllegroHand in-hand reorientation, compute_hand_reward
findings.criterion: Success and failure are hard threshold gates inside the jit reward function. Success: `goal_resets = torch.where(torch.abs(rot_dist) <= success_tolerance, torch.ones_like(reset_goal_buf), reset_goal_buf)`; on success the goal is resampled, `successes = successes + goal_resets`, and `reward = torch.where(goal_resets == 1, reward + reach_goal_bonus, reward)`. Failure/reset: `resets = torch.where(goal_dist >= fall_dist, torch.ones_like(reset_buf), reset_buf)` (object fell too far from goal) plus timeout `timed_out = progress_buf >= max_episode_length - 1`; optional `resets = torch.where(successes >= max_consecutive_successes, ...)` gate. The reported headline metric is `consecutive_successes` — an exponential moving average (av_factor) of successes-at-reset — exposed via `self.extras['consecutive_successes']`. For pen object the tolerance is doubled: `if ignore_z_rot: success_tolerance = 2.0 * success_tolerance`.
findings.thresholds: successTolerance = 0.1 (rad, orientation geodesic distance rot_dist); reachGoalBonus = 250; fallDistance = 0.24 m; fallPenalty = 0.0; maxConsecutiveSuccesses = 0 (disabled by default); episodeLength = 600 control steps (controlFrequencyInv=2, dt=1/60 => 30 Hz => 20 s); av_factor default 0.1

findings.source: isaac-sim/IsaacLab — reward shaping vs. success gate distinction in the same lift task (dense terms are NOT scorecard, but they are gated by the same thresholds)
findings.criterion: The dense shaping terms are continuous kernels, not gates: `object_ee_distance` returns `1 - torch.tanh(object_ee_distance / std)` (std=0.1), and `object_goal_distance.__call__` returns `is_lifted.float() * (1 - torch.tanh(distance / std))` — i.e., the continuous goal-tracking reward is multiplicatively masked by the SAME binary lift gate (`object_pos_w[:, 2] > minimal_height`). So even the dense reward channel is zeroed unless the 0.04 m height threshold is met. Net structure: dense distance kernels + binary threshold gates + threshold-based terminations; the evaluation-facing number (`Metrics/success_rate`) is purely binary/threshold-based.
findings.thresholds: tanh kernel std: 0.1 (reach), 0.3 (goal coarse), 0.05 (goal fine); binary mask threshold minimal_height = 0.04 m applied to all goal-tracking reward; action_rate_l2 and joint_vel_l2 penalties weight -1e-4 escalated to -1e-1 by curriculum after num_steps=10000

isaac.summary: Verified from primary sources (GitHub API blobs, base64-decoded, exact code quoted). YES — both Isaac Lab and legacy Isaac Gym envs judge manipulation/lift/grasp outcomes with threshold-based binary gates (a scorecard), not graded/continuous verdicts. (1) Isaac Lab lift task (release/3.0.0-beta2 @ 6a7acb0): success = sticky binary `is_lifted & (distance < success_threshold)` with minimal_height=0.04 m and success_threshold=0.05 m, logged as `Metrics/success_rate`; the lift reward itself is a hard `torch.where(z > 0.04, 1.0, 0.0)` gate. (2) Terminations are threshold gates: `object_dropping` fires when object root z < -0.05 m (`root_height_below_minimum`), plus step-count `time_out` at episode_length_s=5.0; goal command resampling_time_range=(5.0,5.0) fixes one goal per episode; core terminations.py also ships `command_resample`, `illegal_contact` (force > threshold), `bad_orientation` (angle > limit_angle) — all threshold gates. (3) Legacy IsaacGymEnvs AllegroHand (main @ aeed298, release 1.5.1): success = `|rot_dist| <= successTolerance` (0.1 rad) → +reachGoalBonus 250 and goal resample; reset = `goal_dist >= fallDistance` (0.24 m) or timeout (600 steps); headline metric = EMA `consecutive_successes`. (4) Dense shaping exists (tanh kernels) but the goal-tracking reward is multiplicatively masked by the same 0.04 m binary lift gate, and the evaluation-facing metric is purely binary. NVIDIA-source category distinction: every one of these numbers (0.04, 0.05, -0.05, 5.0 s, 0.1 rad, 0.24 m, 600 steps, bonus 250) is a PROJECT-AUTHORED task-config value (env cfg dataclass / Hydra YAML) that users may override; none is a PhysX/Kit engine hard limit. Engine-level entries in the same files (PhysxCfg bounce_threshold_velocity, contact_offset, etc.) configure simulation fidelity and are unrelated to task success semantics.

findings.source: ACRONYM (Eppner, Mousavian, Fox — NVIDIA), 'ACRONYM: A Large-Scale Grasp Dataset Based on Simulation'
findings.criterion: Binary pass/fail physics trial (scorecard gate) in NVIDIA FleX. Verbatim, Sec. III 'Grasp Labelling in Simulation': "We use the physics simulator FleX [23] to evaluate and label each grasp. Objects, gripper palm and fingers are simulated as rigid bodies; gravity is not present. The simulation is initialized with the gripper in the pre-grasp state. ... fingers are closed using a velocity-based controller until a force threshold is reached or the hand is fully closed. Finally, a shaking motion is executed: The hand first moves up and down along its approach direction, then rotates around a line parallel to the prismatic joint axes of the fingers. Afterwards, we record grasp success by testing whether the object is still in contact with both fingers." Also: "Shaking applies disturbances in all directions without assuming a particular gravity direction" and the gravity-free shake "has 91% precision and 93% recall on the successful grasps with gravity." Result: "we simulate 17.744 million grasps, out of which 59.21% (approximately 10.5 million grasps) succeed." Bonus primary-source taxonomy: Table I caption — "Grasp labels are generated either manually, by physics simulation, analytical models (f), or through observation of real-world trials" — where ACRONYM/Jacquard/Kappler are marked physics-simulation and Columbia/Dex-Net/GraspNet are marked f (analytic).
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.09584 — PDF p.3, Section III 'Dataset Generation', paragraph 'Grasp Labelling in Simulation' + Table I caption (p.2); repo https://github.com/NVlabs/acronym (README: 'Grasp markers are colored green/red based on whether the simulation result was a success/failure'). Read directly from saved PDF pages 2-4.
findings.thresholds: Success = binary: object still in contact with BOTH fingers after shake (no numeric displacement threshold; finger closing stops at an unspecified force threshold or full closure). Fixed physics: friction=1.0, density=150 kg/m^3, 2000 grasp proposals/object, gripper=Franka Panda 8cm aperture; 59.21% of 17.744M grasps labeled success; shake-vs-gravity agreement 91% precision / 93% recall.

findings.source: DexGraspNet paper (Wang, Zhang, Liu et al., PKU-EPIC), Section III-C 'Grasp Validation'
findings.criterion: Binary two-gate scorecard in Isaac Gym. Verbatim, Sec. III-C: "we validate all of the grasps in a physical simulator Isaac Gym [13] with PhysX as the basic physics engine. We first initialize the gripper using the final grasp parameters. Then, in order to apply active forces on the object, we slightly move each contacting link of the gripper along the normal of its contact point, and set the moved pose as target positions for position control. Finally, gravity with a magnitude of 9.8m/s^2 is added to the scene. A grasp is considered successful if the gripper is still in contact with the object after 100 simulation steps under all 6 axis-aligned directions of gravity. ... if the max penetration depth exceeds 0.1cm, we also consider the grasp as a failure. We only save those grasps who pass both the simulation validation and the penetration validation in our dataset." NOTE (correction to the question's premise): the paper's dataset gate is CONTACT-PERSISTENCE under 6 gravity directions, not 'object displacement below threshold'. Benchmark relaxation, Sec. V-B verbatim: "We adopt an easier criterion (the criterion in Sec. III-C is too strict for the baselines): a grasp is considered valid if it can withstand at least one of the six gravity directions and has a maximal penetration less than 5mm."
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.02697 — PDF p.4 (Sec. III-C Grasp Validation) and p.6 (Sec. V-B Experiments and Results). Read directly from saved PDF pages 3-6.
findings.thresholds: Dataset label: contact persists after 100 sim steps in ALL 6 axis-aligned gravity directions AND max penetration depth < 0.1 cm; gravity 9.8 m/s^2. findings.source: GraspIt! (Miller & Allen, Columbia) — the OLDER analytic tradition: epsilon/volume force-closure quality, no physics trial
findings.criterion: Continuous analytic quality scores computed from the convex hull of contact wrenches — scoring WITHOUT any physics trial or threshold gate. Verbatim, Sec. 3.3 'Computing Grasp Quality': "W = ConvexHull(U_{i=1..n} {w_i,1,...,w_i,m}) (1). If this convex hull contains the wrench space origin then the grasp is stable. One quality measure that is often proposed is the radius, e, of the largest 6D ball, centered at the origin, that can be enclosed with the hull. ... In this worst case the sum magnitude of the contact wrenches would have to be 1/e times the magnitude of the disturbance wrench. The closer e is to 1 the more efficient the grasp is. However, this measure is not invariant to the choice of torque origin as Li and Sastry point out, so the volume v of the convex hull can be used as an invariant average case quality measure for the grasp." Sec. 3.4: "The minimum offset value gives us e ... Qhull can also be queried for the volume of the computed hull which gives us v." That no physics trial occurs is explicit in Sec. 3.2: "Throughout the simulation the object remains fixed with its center of gravity on the WCS origin" — the object is never perturbed; quality derives from Ferrari-Canny wrench-space geometry (their ref [4]).

findings.source: GraspNet-1Billion (Fang, Wang, Gou, Lu, CVPR 2020) — analytic force-closure labels, no simulation trial
findings.criterion: Grasp labels are graded ANALYTICALLY on the mesh, with no physics trial. Verbatim, Data Annotation section: "Grasp candidates are searched in a two dimensional grid D x A, where D is the set of gripper depths and A is the set of in-plane rotation angles. ... Each grasp candidate will be assigned a confidence score based on the mesh model. We adopt an analytic computation method to grade each grasp. The force-closure metric [20, 24] has been proved effective in grasp evaluation: given a grasp pose, the associated object and a friction coefficient mu, force-closure metric outputs a binary label indicating whether the grasp is antipodal under that coefficient. The result is computed based on physical rules, which is robust. ... With delta-mu = 0.1 as interval, we increase mu gradually from 0.1 to 1 step by step until the grasp is antipodal. The grasp with lower friction coefficient mu has more probability of success. Thus we define our score s as: s = 1.1 - mu, (2) such that s lies in (0, 1]." Also: "the ratio of positive and negative labels in our dataset is around 1:2", and Sec. 3.5: for test-time evaluation "we do not pre-compute labels for the test set, but directly evaluate them by calculating the quality score using force closure metric [20]". So the label is a graded analytic score from a mu-sweep of binary antipodal (force-closure) checks — the analytic tradition, not a displacement/shaking trial gate.
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.13470 — PDF p.4 (Data Annotation, Eq. 2) and p.5 (Sec. 3.5 Discussion); real-robot corroboration Table 2 (s=1 grasps ~96% real success vs s=0.1 ~14%). Read directly from saved PDF pages 4-6. Cross-corroborated by ACRONYM Table I labeling GraspNet's label type as 'f' (analytical models).
findings.thresholds: mu swept 0.1 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1; score s = 1.1 - mu, s in (0,1] (11-level discrete analytic grade, not a sim pass/fail gate); positive:negative ~ 1:2; collision check removes invalid poses; evaluation AP averages Precision@k for mu = 0.1..0.5.

datasets.summary: Verified from primary sources (paper PDFs read page-by-page + repo code read line-by-line): YES — when grasp datasets are labeled in physics simulation, the labels are binary threshold-gate 'scorecard' outcomes of a simulated trial. ACRONYM (NVIDIA, FleX): close fingers to a force threshold, execute a shaking motion (up/down along approach, then rotation about the finger-joint axis; no gravity), success iff the object is still in contact with both fingers — 59.21% of 17.744M grasps pass. DexGraspNet (Isaac Gym): success iff hand-object contact persists after 100 sim steps under ALL 6 axis-aligned gravity directions AND max penetration < 0.1 cm; the code implements exactly this (sum(result)==6 gate + E_pen < 0.001 m gate). In contrast, the older analytic tradition scores grasps WITHOUT any physics trial: GraspIt! computes continuous epsilon (radius of largest origin-centered ball in the contact-wrench convex hull) and volume v while 'the object remains fixed' — pure Ferrari-Canny wrench-space geometry; GraspNet-1Billion assigns analytic force-closure labels by sweeping friction coefficient mu from 0.1 to 1.0 (step 0.1) until the grasp is antipodal and scoring s = 1.1 - mu — a graded analytic score, not a trial gate. ACRONYM's own Table I is primary-source confirmation of this taxonomy, explicitly splitting datasets into labels 'by physics simulation' (ACRONYM, Jacquard, Kappler) vs 'analytical models' (Columbia, Dex-Net, GraspNet). So: sim-labeled datasets = scorecard threshold gates on trial outcomes; analytic-labeled datasets = continuous/graded quality scores computed geometrically.
datasets.caveats: (1) Correction to the question's premise on DexGraspNet: the dataset gate is CONTACT-PERSISTENCE under 6 gravity directions + penetration < 0.1cm — not 'displacement below threshold'. A displacement parameter (threshold_dis=0.1) exists in isaac_validator.py but is never used in the success logic; dis_move=0.001 is a 1mm active-squeeze perturbation applied before simulation, not a gate. External force is applied via 6 gravity directions (scene rotated against fixed gravity) plus the position-control squeeze, not explicit force vectors. (2) GraspNet-1Billion was verified from arXiv:1912.13470 (Dec 2019 version) because the CVPR 2020 CVF openaccess PDF returned HTTP 403; section numbering in the camera-ready may differ (annotation text is substantively identical; the CVPR version reports 1.1B grasps vs 370M in this version's Table 1). (4) ACRONYM's finger-closing 'force threshold' numeric value is not stated in the paper. (5) DexGraspNet repo code line numbers refer to the main branch as fetched 2026-08-06 (file headers 2023-02). findings.source: Kappler, Bohg, Schaal, "Leveraging Big Data for Grasp Planning", ICRA 2015 (~500,000 sim-generated grasps, 700+ objects, 80+ categories)
findings.criterion: Grasp labeled stable/unstable by two competing gates: the classic epsilon-metric (threshold on force-closure wrench-space quality) vs a physics-simulation shake-test metric; labels then compared against crowdsourced human predictions of grasp success. Result: epsilon-metric labels are noisier and a LESS consistent predictor of grasp success than the physics metric — i.e., the same grasp flips pass/fail depending on which analytic threshold gate is used. Caveat: ground truth here is human judgment, not real-robot execution.
findings.citation: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7139793/ (abstract); project index https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Leveraging-big-data-for-grasp-planning-Kappler-Bohg/65e9a1bc823bb390b3b6b2e1c40468c4e4c980f9 — abstract states physics-metric labels "less noisy than those from the epsilon-metric" and physics-metric "more consistent predictor for grasp success than the epsilon-metric"
findings.thresholds: ~500,000 labeled grasps; >700 objects; >80 categories; no single universal epsilon cutoff survives — the paper's point is that the epsilon threshold gate itself is the unreliable component

findings.source: Li et al., "Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation" (SIMPLER), CoRL 2024, arXiv:2405.05941
findings.criterion: Sim task-success rate used as proxy scorecard for real-robot policy success. Key limit finding: raw simulated success rates do NOT match real absolute numbers; the authors explicitly abandon Pearson correlation on absolute success and introduce Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) because only policy RANKINGS, not absolute pass rates, transfer. Correlation with real outcomes is achieved only after deliberately mitigating "control and visual disparities between real and simulated environments" (system identification, green-screen visual matching) — naive sim environments without these mitigations are unreliable evaluators.
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05941 (abstract: identifies control/visual gaps as key challenges, proposes mitigation approaches); https://simpler-env.github.io/ (1500+ paired sim-and-real evaluations, 2 embodiments, 8 task families; MMRV motivation)
findings.thresholds: 1500+ paired sim/real evaluations; MMRV (lower=better) replaces Pearson on absolute success rates; no fixed numeric pass threshold transfers sim-to-real

findings.source: Wei et al., "Approximate Convex Decomposition for 3D Meshes with Collision-Aware Concavity and Tree Search" (CoACD), ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH 2022, arXiv:2205.02961
findings.criterion: Direct demonstration that convex-hull/coarse convex-decomposition collision geometry fabricates contacts and flips sim manipulation pass/fail verdicts independent of the policy: Sec 4.1 — with convex hulls "robots can no longer grasp the scissors by the circles... can no longer interact with the water dispenser"; solid hulls make "water particles collide with the interior of the teapot" (cavity filled = false contact volume). Sec 7.3 OpenCabinetDrawer experiment — "when using V-HACD's collision shapes, the robot arm easily slips off the handles, since they fill the holes": identical task/policy scores 49% success with V-HACD collision meshes vs 80% with CoACD. A 31-percentage-point swing in a binary sim success scorecard caused purely by the collision-decomposition artifact.
findings.citation: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.02961 Sec 4.1 (concavity/false-contact examples) and Sec 7.3 (OpenCabinetDrawer 49% vs 80%); arXiv abstract notes hulls "fail to preserve fine-grained details (e.g., filling a toaster's slots)"
findings.thresholds: V-HACD 49% vs CoACD 80% task success on OpenCabinetDrawer (31 pp gap from collision geometry alone)

findings.source: Narang et al. (NVIDIA), "Factory: Fast Contact for Robotic Assembly", RSS 2022, arXiv:2205.03532 — NVIDIA primary source for PhysX/Isaac Gym contact generation
findings.criterion: Engine-level (not scorecard) evidence from NVIDIA itself: convex decompositions "can produce spatial artifacts on complex geometries", and even perfect decompositions scale O(n^2) in collision pairs during contact generation. This is NVIDIA's stated motivation for replacing convex-decomposition collision with voxel-based SDF collision for contact-rich tasks in Isaac Gym — i.e., the vendor of PhysX documents that convex-decomposition contact geometry is an artifact-prone approximation for tight-tolerance contact reasoning.
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.03532 / https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss18/p035.pdf (geometric-representations discussion, Sec II-III); companion doc https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacGymEnvs/blob/main/docs/factory.md
findings.thresholds: O(n^2) collision-pair scaling with n convex pieces; no numeric gate — qualitative artifact warning from the engine vendor

findings.source: Gunes et al. (survey), "Reproducibility in Human-Robot Interaction: Furthering the Science of HRI", Current Robotics Reports, 2022
findings.criterion: Honest answer to the preregistration question: preregistration of predictions/analyses before running experiments is RARE in robotics. The only robotics subfield with a visible preregistration practice is HRI (human-subject side): the survey reports "there have not been many preregistrations of HRI studies in total" on OSF, though the count has been increasing over ~3 years; ACM/IEEE HRI added a Reproducibility theme only in 2020. I found no evidence of preregistration norms in manipulation/sim-evaluation robotics — the closest analogues are fixed benchmark protocols (YCB, RoboCup, cloud benchmarks like QBIT arXiv:2503.07479), which standardize procedure but do not preregister per-experiment predictions or tolerances.
findings.citation: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43154-022-00094-5 (also https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9589714/) — preregistration definition + OSF count remarks; replicability-crisis companion: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8961736/
findings.thresholds: No numeric thresholds; qualitative prevalence claim (“not many... in total”, increasing over last 3 years)

findings.source: Two independent papers arguing binary success metrics hide failure modes: (a) RoboEval, arXiv:2507.00435; (b) Xu et al., "Beyond Binary Success: A Diagnostic Meta-Evaluation Framework for Fine-Grained Manipulation", arXiv:2605.19986
findings.criterion: (a) RoboEval abstract verbatim: "Existing evaluations often collapse performance into outcome counts, masking differences in execution quality and obscuring failure structure" — two policies with identical binary success rates can be one fluent/robust and one brittle/erratic yet indistinguishable under pass/fail scoring; proposes stagewise progress tracing and failure-mode localization instead. (b) Beyond Binary Success abstract: benchmarks that "collapse these capacities into binary success rates" are "systematically inflating reported capabilities by up to 70% and masking the architectural bottlenecks that impede real-world deployment".
findings.citation: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00435 + https://robo-eval.github.io/media/RoboEval.pdf (abstract; 8 bimanual tasks, 3000+ demonstrations); https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19986 (abstract, "up to 70%" inflation claim)
findings.thresholds: Reported capability inflation up to 70% when collapsing to binary success (arXiv:2605.19986 abstract); RoboEval: 8 tasks, >3000 demos
findings.version_or_date: RoboEval arXiv July 2025; Beyond Binary Success arXiv May 2026 (preprint, peer-review status unverified)

counter.summary: COUNTER-lens result: primary-source evidence exists on all four hunted axes against over-trusting threshold/gate pass-fail scoring in physics-sim grasp evaluation. (1) Label-validity: Kappler ICRA 2015 shows the classic epsilon-threshold grasp gate produces noisy, inconsistent labels (physics shake-test better, but validated against crowdsourced human judgment, not real robots); SIMPLER (CoRL 2024) shows sim success rates only rank-correlate with real-robot outcomes after deliberate control/visual gap mitigation, and absolute sim pass rates do not transfer (hence their MMRV metric). (2) Collision geometry: CoACD (SIGGRAPH 2022) gives the sharpest number — the identical sim manipulation task scores 49% vs 80% success purely from V-HACD vs CoACD convex decomposition ("they fill the holes"), and NVIDIA's own Factory paper (RSS 2022) states convex decompositions "produce spatial artifacts" in PhysX/Isaac contact generation — directly relevant to any Isaac convex-decomposition grasp gate: a sim GRASP_FAIL can be a geometry artifact, and a sim GRASP_PASS is not real-robot truth. (3) Preregistration is genuinely rare in robotics — visible only in HRI (small but growing OSF counts per Current Robotics Reports 2022); no manipulation-community preregistration norm found, so per-experiment prediction/tolerance preregistration exceeds field practice. (4) Two papers (RoboEval 2025; Beyond Binary Success 2026, claiming up to 70% capability inflation) argue binary success collapses distinct failure modes and masks brittleness. Net counter-lens implication: threshold-gate sim verdicts are decision tools, not ground truth — their strongest documented failure mode is exactly collision-decomposition-induced false contact, and their outputs should be read as rankings/diagnostics rather than real-world success claims.
counter.caveats: 1) Kappler et al. validates sim metrics against crowdsourced HUMAN success predictions, not physical robot trials — I did not verify a large-N sim-label-vs-real-robot correlation study within budget (candidates like Goins et al. 2014, ~522 real grasps, and Rubert et al. IROS 2017 surfaced in search results but were not fetched/verified; treat as leads only). 2) "Beyond Binary Success" (arXiv:2605.19986) is a 2026 preprint; the "up to 70%" inflation figure comes from its abstract and its peer-review status is unverified. 3) MPI publisher pages for Kappler DNS-failed and Semantic Scholar API was rate-limited (HTTP 429); the Kappler abstract claims were confirmed via two independent search-index renderings of the abstract rather than the publisher page. 4) CoACD Sec 4.1/7.3 quotes and the 49%/80% numbers came via an ar5iv fetch summarized by an intermediate model; wording is quoted as returned and section numbers should be spot-checked before formal citation. 5) The Factory "spatial artifacts" phrasing was confirmed via search-result rendering of the paper text, not a direct PDF read. 6) All web fetches occurred 2026-08-06; arXiv HTML availability varies by paper version.

dAdv.position: When both Arm-F and Arm-D produce GRASP_PASS, the adopted canonical asset should be D (plug disabled + distal fingers authored), provided a small set of preregistered guards pass. The plug (link5 part_029/030, protruding to TCP−4.458mm at r=11.77mm) is a proven phantom: D424 established that the frozen attempt3 asset makes top-down grasping geometrically impossible while the real gripper succeeded at rim pinch with 0-12mm bite (T1), i.e., a demonstrated sim/real mismatch. The asset's entire remaining purpose after T3 is fidelity to the real gripper — the pipeline's very next step after adoption is T4 real reproduction comparison (START_HERE.md:49, 24th doc §5 step 6). Canonicalizing F means permanently carrying a known-false structure whose avoidance requires a standing hover-margin workaround (margin ≥ +4.5mm, bite depth x=L−m capped at roughly 5-9mm vs the real 0-12mm band), which every future prereg (T5 hold-move-place, T6 randomization, T7 RL) must inherit, and whose phantom contacts would corrupt exactly the exploratory trajectory classes T6/T7 generate. The factorial design (B,F,D full matrix, preregistered) already delivers causal attribution, so F's 'minimal diff' evidential advantage is consumed at the moment of the tie — it does not need to be embodied in the go-forward asset. D's known side effect (fixed-jaw seed-plane coverage thinning from 4 carriers to 2: 027/031 remain) is real but measurable, already preregistered as a quantified check with a discriminator anchor, and — decisively — empirically testable by direct F-vs-D contact-observable comparison on the identical tuple, which is stronger evidence than the coverage metric itself. Verdict: CONDITIONAL_D, with the tie-break revised in the prereg BEFORE any Isaac run (the current F-default tie-break is only a pending proposal awaiting user confirmation ②, 24th doc §6 — switching it post hoc after seeing results would be exactly the override behavior this design forbids).
strongest_arguments: FIDELITY IS THE ASSET'S JOB AND T4 IS NEXT: Adoption immediately feeds T4 real reproduction comparison (24th doc:80 '조합 표 판정 → 채택 자산 확정 → T4 실물 재현 대조'; START_HERE.md:49). D424 proved the plug contradicts reality: sim top-down grasp 'geometrically impossible' on attempt3 vs T1 real rim pinch 0-12mm success = '정면 모순 → sim 조/목구멍 충돌 형상의 실물 불일치 실증' (DECISIONS.md:25362-25367). Adopting F canonicalizes a confirmed-false structure into the exact asset whose next task is a real-vs-sim comparison; any T4 discrepancy then carries a permanent confounder ('physics gap or retained phantom?'). With D that explanation class is eliminated by construction.

F'S PASS IS ONLY A SUB-BAND CERTIFICATE UNDER A WORKAROUND: The FATAL finding showed F's original plug-stop premise contradicted the GRASP_PASS contract (descend target miss = APPROACH_FAIL inheritance, t3_prereg.md:10-12,133; 24th doc:42), so F was redesigned to NEVER let the plug contact: hover tuple margin>=+4.5mm, x=L−m, recommended L=9.5-13.5mm giving bite x≈5-9mm vs real T1 band 0-12mm (24th doc:42). F-canonical therefore permanently excludes the shallow-margin and deep-bite regimes the real gripper demonstrably reaches, and every future prereg must carry the hover-margin guard as a non-physical, artifact-avoidance constraint.

PHANTOM CONTACTS POISON T6/T7: The ladder ahead is T5 hold-move-place, T6 position randomization, T7 RL (DECISIONS.md:25122-25126). Randomization and RL explore trajectories by design; any exploration bringing TCP within 4.458mm of the object top over r≈11.77mm (DECISIONS.md:25395-25396) hits a structure absent on the real robot, injecting reward/contact signals that cannot transfer. D424's own new adoption gate ('충돌 자산 채택 게이트에 조 간극-깊이 검증 추가', DECISIONS.md:25370-25371) exists to exclude throat occlusion; F does not cure the occlusion, it merely schedules trajectories around it — F passes the letter of T3 while violating the spirit of the D424 gate.

CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION IS ALREADY BANKED — 'MINIMAL DIFF' ADDS NOTHING POST-TIE: The preregistered (B,F,D)×{pass, fail-consistent, off-prediction} full matrix (24th doc:44) plus B's negative-control prediction (plug removal alone insufficient — distal fingers absent, DECISIONS.md:25405-25407) and the a1/a4 identical stop-z signature (DECISIONS.md:25355-25361) fully characterize the plug's causal role. Once F and D both pass in-prediction, keeping the plug 'for conservatism' preserves zero additional inferential power; conservatism about a structure already proven phantom is preservation of a known error, not caution.

VARIABLE LADDER MAKES THE DEFERRED SWAP THE EXPENSIVE PATH: AGENTS.md:90-99 (only 1-2 new variables per case; folders forward-only). If F is adopted and the plug must be removed later at T5/T6 when it interferes, that swap is a new mid-ladder variable invalidating all F-baseline comparisons and forcing re-verification of T4 results against a changed asset. Adopting D now pays the swap cost exactly once, at the cheapest point — before any T4 baseline exists.

D'S SIDE EFFECT IS BOUNDED AND PREREGISTERED; F'S RETAINED DEFECT IS UNBOUNDED: P-removal thins fixed-jaw seed-plane coverage from 4 carriers (027/029/030/031) to 2 (027/031), but this is already preregistered as a quantified residual-coverage check with an explicit discriminator anchor for 'F insufficient vs P-removal side effect' (24th doc:49). The plug's future interference surface across all T5-T7 trajectory classes is unquantifiable in advance. A measured, gated risk beats an open-ended one.

ADOPTING D LOSES NOTHING — F IS PRESERVED AS DIAGNOSTIC CONTRAST: Non-adopted assets are preserved (forward-only, AGENTS.md:99; attempt3 original frozen with derived copies allowed, START_HERE.md:75). If T4 shows an off-prediction discrepancy localizing to fixed-jaw contact, F remains fully provenanced for a contrast rerun. The reverse (adopt F, shelve D) gives no diagnostic leverage on phantom-contact anomalies because F itself contains the confounder.
attack_on_opposite: F-DEFAULT CONFLATES TWO DIFFERENT DECISIONS: The tie-break rationale '최보수' (most conservative, 24th doc:44) is a claim about causal inference cleanliness WITHIN T3 — F is indeed the cleanest single-factor cell. But adoption is a decision about the OPERATING ASSET for T4-T7, which is a fidelity question. Exporting a T3 inference heuristic into the canonical asset for real-world comparison is a category error of the same species the review itself flagged in repair row 3 (24th doc:44, '판정 매트릭스 오류 — 범주 오류').

F IS NOT CONSERVATIVE ABOUT REALITY — ONLY ABOUT THE FROZEN ASSET: 'Minimal diff' is measured against attempt3, an asset already convicted of two defects (D424/D425; START_HERE.md:12-13). Minimality should be measured against the validation target — the real gripper — and by that metric D is the minimal-diff asset: it removes a structure absent in reality and adds structures present in reality. F preserves maximal diff from the real gripper at the exact location (jaw throat) where the mismatch was proven.

F'S CONSERVATISM IS CONDITIONAL ON A PERMANENT WORKAROUND WITH A STANDING FAILURE MODE: F only passes because the redesign guarantees the plug never contacts (24th doc:42). Every future tuple must carry margin>=+4.5mm; one authoring slip below threshold yields an APPROACH_FAIL that mimics a physics failure but is actually phantom contact — a standing misattribution hazard of precisely the kind the 24th design's hallucination-blocking machinery (24th doc:53-63) was built to structurally eliminate. F-default institutionalizes that hazard indefinitely.

F'S CERTIFIED ENVELOPE IS STRICTLY NARROWER AT EQUAL COST: At the shared preregistered tuple, F and D certify the same grasp; but F is certified ONLY on bite x≈5-9mm while reality demonstrated 0-12mm (24th doc:42; DECISIONS.md:25364). An asset validated on a sub-band with a known phantom guarding the remainder is LESS validated with respect to reality, not more. F-default buys no fidelity at the certified point and forfeits fidelity everywhere else.

THE FACTORIAL DESIGN F-DEFAULT LEANS ON WAS BUILT TO INDICT THE PLUG: B exists as a negative control precisely because plug-removal-alone is predicted insufficient (DECISIONS.md:25405-25407). If B fails in-prediction and F/D pass in-prediction, the two-component model (phantom plug + missing fingers) is confirmed on all three cells. At that evidentiary state, retaining the plug retains a component the experiment just re-confirmed as false. If instead B unexpectedly passes, the design already mandates full stop and model refutation (24th doc:44) — so there is no branch in which the plug earns canonical status on evidence.

F-DEFAULT IS NOT YET RATIFIED, SO ARGUING D NOW IS PROCEDURALLY CLEAN: The F tie-break is pending user confirmation ② (24th doc:86-88) — it is a lead proposal, not a decided rule. Choosing D-default in the prereg before any Isaac run costs nothing procedurally; choosing F now and swapping later costs a Variable Ladder violation-priced asset change (AGENTS.md:92).
